She awoke, in a misty grove where the ground lay cold and lifeless, the grass beneath her seemed unusually ethereal, moving with the wind but ignoring the presence of her curious hands, soon touching the dirt to bring her up, noting that she was alone in the forested plain, and begins to walk amongst the trees, who seemed to converse with each other as the girl moved. She looked back while moving forward, and as she did the trees' conversations were replaced by a strange humming, and she then tripped over a large root. She looked up in awe of the behemoth that lay before her, its bright blue leaves caressing the sky as the humming came to an abrupt end, its echoing chiming across the flatlands. "Hello, I am Kind, What is your name?" I... I'm Charlotte, but my daddy calls me Charlie." A small, butterfly-like creature flew in from behind Kind, lightly landing on Charlottes' nose, singing gleefully as the tree spoke once more. "This is Eve, she's been quite lonely as of late." "Hello Eve." Eve laughs, but says nothing, throwing a strange glowing dust on a flower, which casts a shadow in turn, which draws Charlottes' attention towards the small, vegetative creature. Soon all of her attention lay on the shadow, which despite only existing for a few quick moments, its image was forever kept in the young girl's thought. She heard powerful drums and devilish violins, almost feeling the shadow dance around in her mind as its memory subsides into the subconscious, and despite a feeling of doubtful fear, she giggles at the tickling of the fairies' wings. "What has brought you here, Charlie?" "I... don't know, I feel lost." "Don't feel lost child, You are where she would want you to be." "But, I'm afraid of the forest, it's too big." "Don't feel afraid child, You are where she would want you to be." "Who's she?" The sky visibly darkened and the mist thickened, making it impossible to see Kind or its friend Eve, and as this happened, Charlotte ran forward to grasp the great tree, but found nothing but empty space, falling to the ground and scraping her knee. She cried out as her blood began to surge out of the small injury, stopping her weeping only when she heard a rustling noise nearing itself to her presence. "Who's there?" She cried, as the rustling became louder, seemingly coming from all directions. She saw red glowing eyes in the darkness, and a growling coming from a single pair in front of her, she yelled. "Stop! Go away!" But the crimson lights that stared at her did not fade, rather, became closer, and in fear Charlie closed her eyes, crying. "I want to go home!" She yelled, not for a second parting her eyelids. Slowly, the growling began to fade away, leaving as it came, with the rustling, soon silence enveloped. Hearing nothing Charlotte opened her eyes, discovering she was no longer surrounded in misty darkness, rather, she was at home, in her bed, alone, the door of her room wide open, as if someone, something had just left.

In order to foster more detailed discussions on particular topics rather than simply discussing articles and news stories as we usually do here, I've decided to start this periodic series in which I will post a new iteration every several days/week/arbitrary period as appropriate on a new, relevant topic. I do not claim to be neutral on any of the topics I will bring up, so I will attempt to ameliorate my bias by letting others have the first word and only espousing my own views after allowing someone else to begin the debate.

I firmly believe that the best way to refine one's views is to test them against criticism and forge them on the anvil of vigorous and diverse debate (hence the title) and to that end I strongly encourage everyone from anarchists to communists and between to participate.

To begin and test this system, in this iteration we'll discuss the minimum wage, a somewhat popular topic in recent months. Some common questions on topic to consider:

  • Should there be a minimum wage(s)?

  • If so, how should it be determined ("poverty line," cost of living, adjustment for inflation, etc.)?

  • Should the minimum wages in the US and in other countries be raised, lowered, or remain the same?

The goal of the minimum wage is to outlaw low paying jobs for the unskilled and inexperienced

The law, simply, says: it is illegal, and therefore criminal, for anyone to hire anyone else below the level of X dollars an hour. This means, plainly and simply, that a large number of free and voluntary wage contracts are now outlawed and hence that there will be a large amount of unemployment.

Remember that the minimum wage law provides no jobs; it only outlaws them; and outlawed jobs ( unemployment ) are the inevitable result.

And let us not forget that the law does not grant to the federal government the power to implement a minimum wage

I'm inclined to agree, especially given the evidence supports your claim that the laws primarily impact unskilled laborers. Over half of people working minimum wage jobs are younger than 25, and most work part-time. This suggests, as one would expect, that the classic "ladder" analogy for work experience is largely correct, as people tend to earn more money as they amass more work experience.

Crucially, that system also lends itself against an enforced minimum wage, which effectively raises the first rung of that proverbial ladder. When teenagers and other young people who have no experience must compete for the same jobs with experienced older people, they predictably will not succeed (and indeed, many young people today claim that it is exceedingly difficult to get a job with no experience).

The obvious solution to this problem in my view is to allow lower wage jobs to exist; skilled workers won't want them, and unskilled workers will work them temporarily to gain experience. Wage demographics suggest that such extremely low wage jobs would be even more disproportionately filled by young people. Those jobs fill a valuable niche in any economy, and making them illegal for the benefit of the small minority of low-wage workers who support families is short-sighted at best.

As for some more scholarly, research-based arguments on the minimum wage, your cited paper appears to suffer from a major flaw: it only examines a single firm, which may have merely been an exception to an overall trend. Any serious inquiry must consider entire regions if not whole countries. To that end, consider this comprehensive study of past work, which found that a veritable mountain of evidence generally supported the claim that young people are less employed as a result of minimum wages.

The effect of the minimum wage on young adult employment is negative and smaller than that for teenagers. This conclusion rests on much less evidence than is available for those 16-19 years. The direction of the effect on adult unemployment is uncertain in the empirical work as it is in theory.

In other words, though there is reasonable disagreement on whether it's bad for older adults (I personally doubt it, as they tend to make more money anyway), the evidence is very strong that young people are hurt by the policy, progressively more so as it is enforced. Indeed, as your own source indicates:

Positive effects occur in markets where the wage floor was only moderately binding

This means that a minimum wage is only helpful when it is not seriously enforced, suggesting that jobs below the minimum wage are indeed vital to a healthy economy.
